newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ SPORT - NZ target weak link in Australian pack.
newsitem.headline: NZ SPORT - NZ target weak link in Australian pack.

text.p: DUNEDIN, Aug 15 - The All Blacks will be spared vital time knocking on the surface to find the weak link in the Wallaby pack in Saturday's sell-out trans-Tasman rugby test at Carisbrook, NZPA reports.
They'll enter the ground before 42,000 with a clear knowledge that the brittle second row should crack if enough pressure was exerted there early.

Though All Black coach John Hart and captain Sean Fitzpatrick declined to pick individual targets in public, the unbeaten home side will undoubtedly give the Wallaby second row, filled by Owen Finegan, who is more accustomed to backrow play,
and newcomer to test rugby John Langford a fair amount of attention.
Another appearing in the Wallaby jersey for the first time is blindside flanker Fili Finau.
Decimated by injuries, the Wallabies look vulnerable all through the pack for the first time in recent years, and it gives the All Blacks a number of targets to exploit.
Langford, captain John Eales' replacement, is a big, strong lock who had a fine Super 12, but he has experienced neither the intensity nor the combination with his front and backrowers.
Harder still is the fact that his game has been restricted to just club level since the ACT Brumbies' Super 12 final against the Auckland Blues 2-1/2 months ago.

The All Blacks' strike rate at exploiting weaknesses in the opponents has been almost 100 percent. An example of that was illustrated at Lancaster Park in the first Bledisloe Cup match where Matt Cockbain made his debut at lock.
Though Cockbain had a fair game around the field, their scrum buckled from the front because of inconsistent application from behind. The All Blacks eventually scored a push-over try in that game.
Another example was the South African midfield where Percy Montgomery's inexperience was exploited by the All Black backline.

However, the way the Australians have gone about their selection, it appears that they would want to keep play well away from the forwards, who, from the outset, seem to lack the grunt to take on the All Blacks head-on.
"I think a wider game suits our team better this time," Wallaby first five-eighth David Knox said.
"If we can keep the ball in front of the forwards we should have enough space to get the ball wide and have the pack playing more of a supporting role. This pack is mobile."

The selection of Andrew Blades at tighthead prop, Finegan in the second row and Finau, Troy Coker and Wilson as the back rowers clearly indicates Wallaby coach Greg Smith's intention to play at high speed like the Springboks did at Ellis Park against the All Blacks.
John Hart, the All Black coach, was aware of two things about the Wallabies.
He believed they could be more dangerous in the face of adversity with the team being ravaged by injuries and the ACT Brumbies' influence in the side.
"I think they'll be more dangerous as a result of that (injuries) because they would have a lot of resolve, guys coming in," Hart said.
The Wallabies lost three members of the pack, lock and captain Eales, flanker Cockbain and No 8 Daniel Manu to injuries this week.
The other frontline players lost earlier include Tim Horan, Pat Howard and Matthew Burke.
Eales' knee injury was the biggest blow to the Australians, and Hart thought that single factor would help bring the Wallabies together, which captain Wilson acknowledged.
Hart said he noticed a similar effect in his team when his captain Sean Fitzpatrick was doubtful for the MCG clash.

"People have sort of written us off already after we lost John Eales. They say we've got no hope at all. That's the way we like it -- with our backs to the wall -- the pressure's come off a little, so there's nothing to lose," Wilson said.
He said the Wallabies exerted pressure on themselves at the MCG as they felt obliged to win to justify the occasion.
"It would have had some bearing on the performances of some of the guys."
Injuries had opened up Wallaby spots for a few more Brumbies players in the team, now with eight of them in all.

The ACT side, which included the influential Coker, halfback George Gregan, first five-eighth David Knox, second-five James Holbeck and winger Joe Roff, all in tomorrow's team, reached the Super 12 final. Their adventurous game was effective and attractive.
The All Blacks picked themselves up after an exhausting week last week when they beat the Springboks 55-35.
By yesterday Hart noticed the fizz was back in the team.
Olo Brown, Fitzpatrick and Craig Dowd will set a new All Black record for front appearances (34th) as a combination, with Brown making his 200th first class appearance.
The team resolved to finish the test season on a high after last week's record victory over the Springboks felt hollow.

"It's the last one of the season and we know there won't be any holding back. Winning tomorrow means winning the tri-series, we don't want have any regrets now when we look back," winger Jeff Wilson said.
